concept.name: Co-location
concept.definition: The placement of a firm's trading servers in or near the exchange's own data center to minimize network latency to the matching engine; the CFTC defines co-location as connectivity solutions hosted by the exchange itself, with third-party equivalents termed proximity hosting.
concept.intuition: Physically sit your computers next to the exchange's computers so your messages arrive before everyone else's.
concept.mechanics: Exchanges rent rack space and cross-connects, typically with equalized cable lengths to equalize latency among co-located customers; regulators require such services to be offered on fair, uniform, and non-discriminatory terms (CFTC co-location rulemaking; SEC oversight of exchange co-location services).
concept.failure_modes: Co-location creates a two-tier speed structure between co-located and remote participants and feeds a costly latency arms race whose social value is contested; it shortens only the last network segment, not decision time or cross-market links.
concept.misconceptions: Co-location is not an unfair secret advantage but a regulated, fee-based exchange service open to all customers on non-discriminatory terms - the debate is about its systemic costs, not its legality.
concept.example: A market-making firm hosts its quoting engines in CME Group's Aurora data center, shaving the network hop between its systems and the Globex matching engine to microseconds.

citations.source: CFTC, Concept Release on Risk Controls and System Safeguards for Automated Trading Environments, 78 FR 56542
citations.section: Part II.A.2 (co-location and proximity hosting definitions, note 23)
